lines: An index fund lets you own hundreds of companies with one purchase, even with ten dollars.
It starts with an index, a list of companies that measures part of the market. The S&P 500 is a list of about five hundred of the biggest U.S. companies.
A fund pools money from many investors. An index fund uses that pool to buy every company on the list instead of picking some. So one share of the fund is a tiny slice of all of them.
The S&P 500 gives bigger companies bigger slices. In early October 2026, about eighty-six cents of every ten dollars went to Nvidia, and the ten biggest companies got about thirty-nine percent.
Index funds come as ETFs, which trade all day like a stock, or as mutual funds, which are priced once a day. Many apps sell pieces of an ETF share, so ten dollars is enough to start.
Every fund charges a yearly fee called the expense ratio. A cheap S&P 500 fund charges three hundredths of a percent, which is three dollars a year on ten thousand dollars.

That sounds tiny, but fees compound against you. With two hundred dollars a month from 1995 to 2024, the same stocks grew to about four hundred thirty thousand dollars at that low fee, and only about three hundred fifty-four thousand at a one point one percent fee.
Active funds have managers who pick stocks to try to beat the index. Over the twenty years through 2024, about ninety-two percent of them did worse than the S&P 500.
It's not bad luck. Before fees, all investors together earn the market's return. After their higher fees, the average picker has to fall behind.
So the recipe is simple. Pick a broad index fund with a low expense ratio, and let it ride. Next, you'll open the account you'd buy it in.
